public_rationale: In 2017, adversarial distractor sentences reduced average reading-comprehension F1 from 75% to 36% across sixteen models; direct human testing found substantially smaller losses [e5]. In 2018, a separate speech-recognition study reported 100% success in making DeepSpeech produce attacker-selected transcriptions in its tested white-box setting [e6]. These studies support repeated substantial weaknesses and observed differences from human behavior during the claimed period [e5, e6]. The difference is not universal: a 2018 study found that adversarial images also influenced time-limited human observers [e7].
limitations: These behavioral results do not establish that human and deep-learning mechanisms are fundamentally unrelated [e5, e6, e7].
The speech study's audio-similarity finding does not provide the same direct human comparison as the reading-comprehension study [e5, e6].
The evidence does not establish human immunity to adversarial attacks [e7].

statement.excerpt: “Adversarial attacks” like these have shown remarkable weakness, time and again, repeatedly establishing that what deep learning systems do just isn’t the same as what people do:

from_speaker: what deep learning systems do just isn’t the same as what people do
our_interpretation: The preceding seven-year discussion supplies the historical period.
Repeatedly means multiple independent demonstrations of substantial vulnerability.
The ordinary testable reading concerns differing behavior on attacked tasks. It does not establish that humans and networks share no computational principles.
criteria.support_condition: Multiple primary studies demonstrate substantial adversarial failures, with evidence that human responses or robustness differ on comparable inputs.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The reported vulnerabilities fail to reproduce, or appropriate human comparisons remove the claimed behavioral differences.
